news_title: Lawmakers question KEBS planned use of 'covert operations' during market inspections - The Standard
efet_title: Lawmakers question KEBS planned use of 'covert operations' during market inspections - The Standard
efet_body:
Lawmakers question KEBS planned use of 'covert operations' during market inspections
By Josphat Thiong’o
|
Sep. 30, 2026
Prefer the Standard on Google
Audio By Vocalize
Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) offices in Nairobi.
[File, Standard]
The Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) is facing criticism from lawmakers over proposed regulations that would allow the quality assurance bureau to conduct “covert operations” during market surveillance.
Members of the National Assembly’s Departmental Committee on Delegated Legislation questioned KEBS on the need for the term, warning that it could create legal and accountability problems for the standards regulator.
The House team chaired by Ainabkoi MP Samuel Chepkonga was scrutinising the draft Standards (Market Surveillance) Regulations, 2026 before their publication.
The proposed market surveillance regulations seek to create uniform procedures for
KEBS investigations
, inspections, sampling, testing and enforcement.
Garissa Township MP Mohamed Dekow questioned why KEBS needed to use the term “covert operations” in the proposed regulations.
To which KEBS officials explained that the measure would allow inspectors to visit vendors without prior notice, buy products and have them tested to determine whether they meet the required standards.
Chepkonga, however, urged the regulator to replace the term with language that clearly reflects its legal mandate.
“You will appear without notice, and KEBS is a public entity that should operate with transparency. You should use impromptu inspections rather than covert operations,” said the chairperson.
The lawmakers also expressed concerns over whether KEBS would be able to conduct effective market surveillance without compromising the rights of businesses.
Samburu County MP Pauline Lenguris said the committee needed to understand the reasons behind some of the enforcement measures proposed in the regulations.
She however, was of the view that giving traders advance notice of inspections could undermine enforcement because some vendors might change their conduct before inspectors arrive.
Kilgoris MP Julius Sunkuli called on KEBS to simplify the language used in the regulations so that ordinary Kenyans can understand their rights and obligations.
His sentiments were lauded by the Committee vice-chairman Robert Gichimu, who noted that the regulations should be accessible to all stakeholders and not only lawyers.
The MPs were considering the draft regulations during a pre-publication scrutiny retreat aimed at determining whether proposed statutory instruments comply with the Constitution, enabling legislation and other written laws.
The committee is also examining the extent to which the proposed rules remain within the powers delegated to the regulator.
Stay informed. Subscribe to our newsletter
The Standards (Market Surveillance) Regulations are among eight sets of draft regulations and orders under scrutiny.
Stay Informed, Stay Empowered: Download the Standard ePaper App!
Others are the Standards (Handling of Conditionally Released and Rejected Imports) Regulations, 2026; Standards (Product Certification) Regulations, 2026; Standards (Testing and Designation of Laboratories) Regulations, 2026; and Standards (Scientific and Industrial Metrology) Regulations, 2026.
The committee is also scrutinising the Fertiliser and Animal Foodstuffs (Fertiliser) Regulations, 2026, the Privileges and Immunities (Ford Foundation) Order, 2026, and draft regulations under the Civil Aviation Act.
The market surveillance regulations
under the purview of KEBS also provide for tracking products through the supply chain and allow for corrective measures, including reworking, recycling, withdrawal and recall of products that fail to meet required standards.
The framework further provides for the release of goods found to be compliant.
The House team subsequently directed KEBS to ensure that enforcement operations are transparent, accountable and firmly grounded in the law. This, the lawmakers argued that this would help protect consumers while also safeguarding the rights of businesses during inspections and enforcement.

High Court rules sale of substandard fertilizer violated farmers’ rights
By
Dzuya Walter
October 07, 2026 05:42 (EAT)
Add as a Preferred
Source on Google
Follow us
Follow on Whatsapp
Follow on Google
Follow on Twitter
Audio By Vocalize
The High Court has ruled that the sale of substandard NPK
fertilizer to farmers under the National Fertilizer Subsidy Programme violated
their constitutional rights.
In a judgment issued on Wednesday, the court also found that
the failure by the Cabinet Secretary responsible for agriculture to constitute
the Fertilizer and Animal Foodstuffs Board of Kenya was unlawful and inconsistent
with the Constitution.
"It has also established that the sale to farmers by the
4th Respondent of fertilizer that did not conform to the declared specification
and the applicable standard violated the farmers' rights under Article 46(1)(a)
and Declarations to that effect are the appropriate relief. The prayer for
compensation cannot be granted," court noted.
The case was filed by the Law Society of Kenya (LSK) following
complaints in March 2024 that fertilizer being distributed to farmers under the
government subsidy programme was substandard or counterfeit.
"The farmers who bought subsidized fertilizer at the 4th
Respondent's depots were consumers. They paid for it, and the 4th Respondent, a
public entity, offered it to them. This court has found that the fertilizer was
not of reasonable quality; it fell far short of the composition declared on the
bag and of the specification the 4th Respondent had tendered for, and it was
confirmed in writing that all of the Kelgreen NPK 10:26:10 it sold was unfit for
distribution. The farmers' economic interests were plainly affected," the judge
ruled.
The court found that the NPK 10:26:10 fertilizer sold during
the 2024 long-rains season did not conform to its declared composition and the
applicable Kenya Standard, KS EAS 912:2019.
The product, sold under the brand name 'Kelgreen,' was
manufactured by the 7th Respondent and supplied to the National Cereals and
Produce Board (NCPB), the 4th Respondent, by the 8th Respondent.
The court noted that complaints from farmers and the media
emerged from about March 18, 2024, prompting the suspension of distribution.
The Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) subsequently suspended
the manufacturer’s standardisation mark permits.
Several officials and individuals linked to the supply of the fertilizer
were later charged before the Kiambu Chief Magistrate’s Court.
However, the LSK had argued that investigations and
prosecutions had been conducted in a piecemeal manner and that not everyone
involved had been brought before the courts.
The High Court rejected a request seeking an order compelling
investigators and prosecutors to investigate and prosecute all individuals
allegedly involved.
The judge held that the decision on whether evidence justified
charging additional suspects fell within the mandate of the Director of Public
Prosecutions (DPP).
“Nothing in this judgment limits the power of those offices to
act on further evidence,” the court said, noting that investigations and
prosecutions could continue in relation to persons not yet before the court.
The court also declined to order compensation for all affected
farmers.
It said the farmers on whose behalf compensation was sought
had not been individually identified, while the losses had neither been proved
nor quantified.
The court further noted that NCPB had indicated that affected
farmers had been provided with replacement or top-dressing fertilizer.
The court said farmers whose losses had not been made good
remained free to pursue individual claims.
The LSK had also sought declarations against senior government
officials, an order stopping further implementation of the National Fertilizer
Subsidy Programme and findings against a National Assembly Select Committee
that had investigated allegations surrounding the programme.
Those prayers were declined.
The court stressed that its judgment did not amount to a
finding of guilt or innocence against any person facing criminal charges in
Kiambu Chief Magistrate’s Criminal Case No. E1240 of 2024.
In its final orders, the court declared that the failure to
constitute the Fertilizer and Animal Foodstuffs Board in accordance with
sections 2A and 2C of the Fertilizers and Animal Foodstuffs Act was unlawful
and inconsistent with Articles 10(2)(c) and 129(2) of the Constitution.
It further declared that the sale of the non-conforming NPK
fertilizer to farmers under the 2024 long rains National Fertilizer Subsidy
Programme violated farmers’ rights under Article 46(1)(a) and (c) of the
Constitution.
The remaining prayers were declined, the court marked the
Notice of Motion dated May 31, 2024 as spent, and ordered each party to bear
its own costs.

news_title: Police seize suspected counterfeit alcohol in crackdown - Citizen Digital
efet_title: Police seize suspected counterfeit alcohol in crackdown - Citizen Digital
efet_body:
Police seize suspected counterfeit alcohol in crackdown
By
Johnson Muriithi
October 09, 2026 11:24 (EAT)
Add as a Preferred
Source on Google
Follow us
Follow on Whatsapp
Follow on Google
Follow on Twitter
Police seize counterfeit alcohol in Kirinyaga on October 8, 2026. /JOHNSON MURIITHI
Audio By Vocalize
Police have seized suspected counterfeit alcohol, empty bottles and sealing equipment during a crackdown at Karii Trading Centre in Kangai Ward, Mwea, Kirinyaga County.
The multi-agency operation, led by Kirinyaga Police Commander Anderson Njagi, began on Thursday afternoon and continued into the night following intelligence from members of the public.
Officers, who were armed with a court-issued search warrant, recovered 87 cartons of assorted alcohol in 200ml bottles, 19 cartons of Dallas-branded alcohol in 200ml bottles, several 750ml Jumbo Ice bottles and four crates of 750ml Santa King Ice bottles.
They also seized 157 empty bottles bearing different brands, two battery chargers suspected to have been used to seal the bottles, two motorcycles without number plates and a Toyota Probox, registration number KBM 379G, suspected to have been used to transport the alcohol.
Njagi said the premises were in poor hygienic condition, raising concerns about the safety of the products.
Police will forward the seized items to the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA), the Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) and the Government Chemist for analysis.
The commander said the premises belonged to a suspect identified as Kabogo, who escaped during the raid and is being pursued by police.
He warned those involved in the illicit alcohol trade that the operation marked the beginning of a wider crackdown.
“Hii ni kionjo tu. Tutapambana nao mpaka we make Kirinyaga clean,” Njagi said.
Meanwhile, some residents called on the government to consider legalising traditional brews, including makabo and muratina, arguing that restrictions on their production had contributed to the spread of counterfeit alcohol.
Led by Michael Mugweru, Charles Kariuki, Josphat Kabuci and Duncan Kimani, the residents said the government should explore regulated production of traditional brews as part of efforts to address the sale of dangerous alcohol.
Peter Gatimu said consumers faced serious risks from counterfeit products.
“Even if you take a drum of makabo you cannot die, but when you take a bottle of this fake alcohol, you cannot even walk a step without lying down,” he said.
Duncan Kimani called for greater cooperation between security agencies, local administrators and residents, saying the fight against illicit alcohol would require a coordinated approach.
He questioned the absence of local administrators during the operation, arguing that their knowledge of the area could help identify those involved in the trade.
However, Pastor Josphat Kabuci opposed the consumption of both illicit alcohol and traditional brews, saying he would support the police operation to stop the distribution of the suspected counterfeit products.
Kabuci claimed the suspect had been distributing the alcohol in Karii for an extended period without intervention.
He said he would work with Njagi and his team to ensure those responsible were brought to justice.
Njagi noted that Karii was also the scene of a deadly alcohol poisoning incident in February 2024, when more than 17 people died after consuming toxic illicit alcohol during what became known as the Kangai tragedy.
The commander thanked residents for providing information that led to the raid and urged them to continue reporting suspected illicit alcohol production and distribution.

news_title: KEBS recognises Bungoma County Assembly with historic ISO certification - KBC Digital
efet_title: KEBS recognises Bungoma County Assembly with historic ISO certification - KBC Digital
efet_body:
SHARE
The County Assembly of Bungoma has made history by becoming the first county assembly in Kenya to achieve ISO 9001:2015 Quality Management System certification. The Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) describes the certification as a significant accomplishment that underscores commitment to enhancing institutional efficiency, accountability, and the quality of public service delivery.
According to KEBS, the certification also acknowledges the Assembly’s dedication to implementing systematic management processes, boosting institutional performance, and embedding continuous improvement across all its operations.
- Advertisement -
The certificate was formally presented at a ceremony attended by KEBS Director General Esther Ngari, who was accompanied by Rono Birgen, North Rift Deputy Director, Eng. Zacharia Lukorito, Director of Standards Development and Trade, and Isabella Lunani, Deputy Director of the Certification Body.
The achievement positions the County Assembly of Bungoma as a national leader in adopting internationally recognised quality management standards within county legislative bodies.
KEBS says ISO 9001:2015 offers organisations a framework for establishing and maintaining effective quality management systems and prioritises consistent processes, performance evaluation, accountability, and ongoing improvement.

KEBS extended its congratulations to the County Assembly of Bungoma for this accomplishment, reiterating its support for both public and private sector institutions in adopting standards that foster quality, operational excellence, and enhanced service delivery.
The agency says the certification also highlights the role of standards in strengthening public institutions by promoting structured processes, consistent performance, and a culture of continuous improvement.
